title: The Standard State for a Gas is an Ideal Gas at 1 Bar
lead: Tables of thermodynamic data for gases all refer to one standard state. Its definition fixes a pressure and an ideal gas, and leaves the temperature open.
notes: The page prints no credit, and nothing was left out.
exercise_notes: The exercise and its solution are AI-written; Bloom level and concept tag were chosen by AI.

exercises.prompt: No real gas is ideal, yet the standard state of every gas is a pure ideal gas at 1 bar. Why define it that way, and why does the definition name no temperature?

answer.hint: Think about how far each real gas departs from ideal behavior at 1 bar.
answer.solution: A real gas at 1 bar is slightly non-ideal, and each gas departs from ideality by a different amount. Referring every gas to the same hypothetical ideal gas at 1 bar gives all of them one baseline, so the corrections for non-ideality are made the same way for every gas. The temperature is left out because data are needed at many temperatures: each value is tabulated at a stated temperature, such as 298.15 K, and the standard state at any other temperature is the ideal gas at 1 bar and that temperature.
